nodes.title: Chain Theory
nodes.subtitle: Only entangled pairs exist
nodes.size: Below all lengths (space is built later)
summary: A new idea by Alex Wissner-Gross (Oct 2026).
Reality = networks of linked tiny quantum units.
Brand new. Not yet tested by others.
details: ## Alex says
"Nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of qudits, some qudits shared, known only by distilling them."
That one sentence is the only input. Alex aims for "no free parameters".
Particles would be "chainmail": finite meshes of these links. "A chain, not a string."
## Our reading
It is like a building made only of linked rings. Everything else is how the rings join.
deeper: A compendium of 100 theorems, 109 conditional theorems and 198 open results (release 0.1).
"Theorem" here often means a check over a finite list of networks, not a proof for all.
That its pieces ARE real physics is called a conjecture by Alex himself.
Peer review. Independent checks. A second number that matches a measurement.
Posted 23–24 Oct 2026. No independent expert review found yet (checked 6 Nov 2026).
Made with a "human-superintelligence collaboration". The author has a financial interest in Physical Superintelligence PBC.

nodes.title: Quantum fields
nodes.subtitle: Standard Model: tested
summary: Every particle is a ripple in a field.
The Standard Model: 17 particles, 3 forces.
Tested extremely precisely.
details: ## Recipe
12 matter fields (6 quarks, 6 leptons) + force fields (gluons, photon, W, Z) + the Higgs field.
## How it works
A field is spread over all space. A ripple of fixed size is a particle.
The rules come from symmetry: SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1).
deeper: Its predictions match experiments, e.g. the electron's magnetism to about 1 part in a trillion.
About 19–26 constants must be measured (masses, strengths). The theory does not explain them.
No gravity. No dark matter. Why 3 generations? Why these masses?

nodes.title: Quantum gravity
nodes.subtitle: Gravity at tiny scales?
summary: Joining gravity with quantum rules.
Ideas: strings, loops, chains…

details: ## Why it matters
At the Planck scale (~10⁻³⁵ m) both gravity and quantum effects are strong.
Our two best theories then disagree.
## Candidates
String theory, loop quantum gravity, causal sets, "spacetime from entanglement", Chain Theory.
deeper: No idea is tested, and none leads by evidence.
Lab tests of "gravity-made entanglement" (tiny diamonds, atoms) are being designed; none done yet. LISA (2035) will listen to black holes merging.
Its gravity results are all graded "open" (Open result 1.9).

nodes.title: Qudits & pairs
nodes.subtitle: The links of the chain
summary: A qudit is a tiny quantum unit with d states.
Two qudits share one perfect entangled state.
That pair is one "link".
details: ## Alex says
A qudit has dimension 2 or more (2 = qubit, 3 = qutrit).
A pair is "maximally entangled": as linked as quantum rules allow.
A shared qudit is the end of 2+ pairs. It carries one copy per pair (because entanglement is "monogamous").
## Recipe
2 qudits → 1 link. Links join at shared qudits → a network.
deeper: A less-than-perfect pair would need smooth, continuous numbers. A fully discrete theory cannot have them.
Monogamy of entanglement and tensor networks (PEPS) are standard quantum information.
That reality is made ONLY of these pairs is the untested part.

nodes.title: Distillation
nodes.subtitle: "To know is to link"
summary: To look at a link, you distill it.
Distilling 2 qudits makes them a new pair.
Time = a count of these acts.
details: ## Alex says
To distill two qudits is to project them onto a perfect pair. One copy, no failure.
A "read" is a distillation at one end of a pair.
What is "known" is only what reads can fix with certainty.
## Like
Entanglement swapping: link 1–2 and 3–4, distill 2 with 3, and now 1–4 is a pair.
deeper: "Time is counted, not assumed." Graded a conditional theorem (box 50.1).
The usual quantum probability rule comes out as an output (Alex grades it conditional).
Entanglement swapping is a real lab effect (since 1998).

A field made space grow by a factor e (~2.7) again and again: at least ~60 times ("e-folds"), ~10²⁶ in all.

Space is flat, the sky is the same everywhere, and the seed ripples have the right pattern.

Rivals: bouncing universes, other early phases.

nodes.title: Forces from one link
nodes.subtitle: Qutrit + qubit symmetry
summary: A qutrit linked to a qubit has a symmetry.
It is the same shape as the Standard Model's.
A striking match. Meaning not yet proven.
details: ## Alex says
Turning the qutrit end gives SU(3). Turning the qubit end gives SU(2). One shared phase gives U(1).
Together: (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆, the exact group of the Standard Model.
Its charge is the hypercharge with Y = 1/6, like the left-handed quark doublet.
deeper: The group S(U(3)×U(2)) ≅ (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆ is known (Baez & Huerta 2010).
Alex's new step is reading it as the symmetry of ONE entangled pair.
Why this pair and not others? How hypercharge becomes electric charge is "beyond the Letter".

nodes.title: Hot Big Bang
nodes.subtitle: Hot, dense, expanding
nodes.size: Today's visible universe was once tiny
summary: 13.8 billion years ago.
Hot, dense, and expanding ever since.
Seen in the afterglow light.
details: ## What it is
Not an explosion in space. Space itself stretching, everywhere.
## Timeline
10⁻¹² s: forces split. 10⁻⁵ s: protons form. 3 min: first nuclei. 380,000 yr: atoms.
deeper: Galaxies move apart (Hubble). The afterglow (CMB). The right amounts of H, He, Li.
The "Hubble tension": two ways of measuring the expansion speed disagree (~67 vs ~73 km/s/Mpc).

nodes.title: Higgs field
nodes.subtitle: Gives tiny particles mass
summary: Its particle was found in 2012.
It gives quarks, electrons, W and Z their mass.
NOT most of YOUR mass (see protons).
details: ## How it gives mass
Particles get mass by coupling to the field's steady value (246 GeV) everywhere in space.
## The numbers
Higgs boson: 125.2 GeV (PDG 2024). Found by ATLAS and CMS at CERN, 4 July 2012.
deeper: Only ~1% of a proton's mass comes from Higgs-given quark masses. ~99% is strong-force energy.
Why these couplings? Is the vacuum stable? Do neutrinos get mass this way? Unknown.
Alex conjectures the Higgs is a "closed hub read" in (4,4) links (conditional).

nodes.title: Chainmail particles
nodes.subtitle: Particles as webs of links
summary: Each particle = a small web of links.
Its insides can't be pulled apart by collisions.
So it looks like a point. Alex's idea.
details: ## Alex says
Particles have no visible parts because their parts are "undistillable", not too small.
Example, the electron web: 9 sites and 10 links. A core triangle of three (3,3) links plus one "hub assembly" (links of types (4,2), (3,2), (4,3), (2,2)).
Muon and tau add more hubs to the same core (the tau is "the third hub on the triangle core"). Alex reads this as 3 generations (conditional 152.1).
## Recipe
Links + shared qudits → closed webs.
deeper: 17 particles drawn on 16 webs: 1 on a theorem, 11 conditional, 2 open, 3 not yet in the release.
"That a web is the named particle is a conjecture."
A neat idea: like knots in chainmail. No mass or charge of a real particle has been derived from a web yet (Thm 176.1).
Prediction: no 4th generation. Fits LEP's count of 3 light neutrinos.

nodes.title: Space & time from links?
nodes.subtitle: (2,2) links → spacetime
summary: Alex: space and time are not given.
They come from counting links and acts.
Conditional results. Not proven.
details: ## Alex says
The Lorentz group (special relativity) appears as the symmetries of a "Hermitian split" (conditional, box 54.1).
Spacetime has 1 time + 3 space directions: "one against three" (a theorem of the networks).
Gravity is "a statement about counting": a metric from the depth of a web, curvature as a graph Laplacian (conditional).
A cosmological term (dark energy?) at the "depth exponent" (conditional).
deeper: "Spacetime from entanglement" (Van Raamsdonk 2010) and gravity from thermodynamics (Jacobson 1995) are real research lines.
No measured gravity number (like G) is derived yet. Much of Part VI (metric, worldline, horizon) is conditional or open.
Alex grades "spacetime from (2,2) links" as an open conjecture, with all four gravity results open (Open result 1.9).

nodes.title: Hot particle soup
nodes.subtitle: All particles, ~10⁻¹² s
nodes.size: The whole universe was hotter than 10¹⁵ K
summary: Right after the Big Bang: pure energy.
Energy turned into particle pairs (E = mc²).

details: ## Recipe
Heat energy → pairs of particles + antiparticles, made and destroyed all the time.
At ~10⁻¹² s (~10¹⁵ K) the Higgs field takes its value: the weak and electric forces split, W, Z, quarks and electrons get mass.
## Randomness
Which particles pop out where is quantum chance.
deeper: The LHC recreates these energies (13.6 TeV ≈ 10¹³ eV per collision).

Mass from the Higgs field. Held by gluons.

3 types: electron, muon, tau. They change type as they fly ("oscillation", Nobel 2015).
deeper: Their masses are not given by the Standard Model. Are they their own antiparticle? Unknown.

4 protons → 1 helium-4 + 26.7 MeV (0.7% of mass becomes energy).

Iron/nickel have the most tightly-bound nuclei. Fusing further costs energy.

summary: 94 found in nature, 24 only made in labs.

details: ## Recipe
Element = Z protons + some neutrons + Z electrons.
Where they come from:
Big Bang: H, He, (Li). Big stars: O to Fe. Dying giants: about half past Fe. Neutron-star crashes: gold, uranium. White dwarfs: most iron.
## The abundance zig-zag

Oddo–Harkins rule: even-proton nuclei are usually more abundant than their odd-proton neighbours. Neutron–proton pairing makes even nuclei more tightly bound and stable, so nuclear physics, not chance, gives this pattern.
deeper: By mass the Sun is ~73% H, ~25% He, ~2% everything else.
Most superheavy elements (104–118) last seconds or less; the longest-lived (dubnium-268) ~16–30 hours (measurements differ).

maths.title: Counting & number
maths.subtitle: Names for how many
summary: Numbers describe size, order and position. Different societies built different symbols and counting systems.
details: What counts as known: A definition or theorem is known mathematics only with explicit assumptions and a valid proof. Checking many examples is not a proof for every case.
Where it began: Counting and measurement developed across many cultures; there is no single inventor of "numbers".

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Place-value notation
maths.subtitle: Position carries value
summary: The value of a digit depends on its position. This makes large numbers and efficient calculation much easier.
details: Examples: Babylonian mathematics used base 60; decimal place value with zero developed in India and travelled through other mathematical traditions.
Careful credit: Place-value systems arose independently in more than one place; the story is not one straight chain of invention.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Arithmetic
summary: Arithmetic combines quantities and reverses those combinations. Its rules are the groundwork for calculation and algebra.
details: The core objects: Whole-number operations, order, divisibility and remainders can be treated rigorously within an axiom system.
Larger systems: Extending whole numbers gives negatives, fractions, decimals, real numbers and complex numbers.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Fractions & ratio
maths.subtitle: Parts of a whole
summary: A rational number is a ratio of two integers, with a nonzero denominator. Ratios compare quantities without needing a whole unit.
details: Equivalent forms: 2/3 and 4/6 name the same rational number. A fraction is a number, not a command to divide a physical object.
Beyond fractions: Numbers such as √2 cannot be written as a ratio of integers; the Greeks studied this tension geometrically.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Zero & negatives
maths.subtitle: Nothing becomes a number
summary: Zero can be a placeholder and a number in its own right. Negative numbers extend calculation below zero.
details: Historical care: Brahmagupta gave arithmetic rules for zero and negatives in 628 CE, but zero as a concept and placeholder has an older, wider history.
Not an inventor claim: No single culture or person should be credited with every aspect of zero.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Real numbers
maths.subtitle: A continuous number line
summary: Real numbers fill the number line, including irrational values. Their completeness makes limits possible.
details: The key property: Every nonempty set of real numbers with an upper bound has a least upper bound. This is completeness.
Constructions: Dedekind cuts and equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences are standard constructions; they are different ways to build the same structure.

sources.title: MacTutor: the real numbers and their history

maths.title: Complex numbers
maths.subtitle: A real part + i × an imaginary part
summary: Complex numbers include i, with i² = −1. They are points in a plane, not "less real" than other mathematical numbers.
details: Why they help: Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a root (the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra).
Geometry: Multiplication by a complex number combines scaling and rotation; Euler's formula links exponentials and trigonometry.

sources.title: MacTutor: the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and complex numbers

maths.title: Euclidean geometry
maths.subtitle: Shape from explicit assumptions
summary: Euclid's Elements organised geometry using definitions, postulates and proofs. Its lasting method matters as much as its individual results.
details: A model of proof: The parallel postulate cannot be replaced silently. Changing it leads to consistent non-Euclidean geometries.
Scope: "Euclidean" does not mean this is the only geometry of the physical universe.

maths.title: Pythagoras’ theorem
maths.subtitle: a² + b² = c²
summary: In a right triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides have the same total area as the square of the hypotenuse.
details: A theorem, not a guess: There are many proofs within Euclidean geometry. The Euclidean assumption is essential.
Historical care: Babylonian mathematics used Pythagorean relationships long before the classical Greek tradition; do not treat the named Greek theorem as the whole history.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Coordinate geometry
maths.subtitle: Geometry meets equations
summary: Coordinates turn geometric objects into equations, and equations back into shapes.
details: Why it matters: Lengths, slopes, conics and motion can now be studied algebraically.
Bridge: This is the route from Euclidean geometry to functions, calculus and vector geometry.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Non-Euclidean geometry
maths.subtitle: The parallel rule can change
summary: Replacing Euclid's parallel postulate produces different consistent geometries. A sphere's shortest paths are one familiar model.
details: What changed: Geometry is about consequences of chosen rules, so "parallel lines" can behave differently in different settings.
Physical link: Later mathematics of curved spaces became essential for general relativity.

maths.title: Trigonometry
maths.subtitle: Angles, triangles & waves
summary: Trigonometry relates angles to lengths, and sine and cosine also describe periodic processes.
details: Unit circle: Cosine and sine give a point's x and y coordinates on the unit circle.
Applications: They describe oscillations, rotations, waves and Fourier analysis — not just triangles.

maths.title: Vectors
maths.subtitle: Size + direction
summary: Vectors describe directed quantities such as displacement, but the abstract idea also includes functions and polynomials.
details: Operations: Addition, scaling, length, dot products and cross products each answer different geometric or physical questions.
Generalisation: A vector space is defined by rules for addition and scalar multiplication, not by arrows alone.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

maths.title: Matrices & linear maps
maths.subtitle: Transform several coordinates
summary: A matrix records how a linear transformation acts on coordinates. Multiplication composes transformations.
details: Order matters: AB need not equal BA. A matrix is not just a rectangular table of numbers; its meaning depends on the chosen bases.
Uses: Linear maps describe rotations, projections, systems of equations and many approximations to nonlinear change.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

maths.title: Linear algebra
maths.subtitle: Flat structure, many dimensions
summary: Linear algebra studies vectors, linear maps and systems of linear equations in any finite or infinite dimension.
details: Core ideas: Linear independence, basis, dimension, rank, eigenvalues and eigenvectors explain what a transformation preserves and changes.
Why it matters: Large datasets, computer graphics, networks and physical models all use this language.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

maths.title: Eigenvalues & spectra
maths.subtitle: Directions that only stretch
summary: An eigenvector keeps its direction under a linear map, while its eigenvalue gives the scale change.
details: Spectra: Spectral theory generalises this idea to operators, including infinite-dimensional settings.
Spectrum has two jobs: It describes linear behaviour, but an operator's spectrum is not just a list of numbers in every infinite-dimensional setting.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)
Encyclopedia of Mathematics: spectrum of an operator

maths.title: Inner products
maths.subtitle: Angles and length, generalised
summary: An inner product supplies lengths, angles and orthogonal projection in a vector space.
details: Dot product is one example: Functions can also be multiplied and integrated to define an inner product.
Limit needed: A complete inner-product space is called a Hilbert space; finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces already satisfy this.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

maths.title: Hilbert spaces
maths.subtitle: Geometry for quantum states
summary: A Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space. It supports orthogonal decompositions and rigorous quantum state spaces.
details: Quantum mechanics: States are represented by vectors (strictly, usually rays) in a Hilbert space; observables use operators.
Caution: The space is a mathematical structure. Physical meaning comes from a model and its rules of interpretation.

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare: Quantum Theory I — mathematical formalism

maths.title: Algebra
maths.subtitle: Letters for unknowns & rules
summary: Algebra uses symbols for arbitrary or unknown quantities, so relationships can be reasoned about independently of a particular value.
details: Not just x: Equation-solving, symbolic manipulation and later abstract structures all belong to algebra.
Historical care: Equation-solving is older than al-Khwārizmī; his work is a major landmark in a much broader global history.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Equations & functions
maths.subtitle: Relations & input–output
summary: An equation states a constraint; a function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain.
details: Keep the meanings distinct: y = x² can define a function; x² + y² = 1 defines a circle but not a single global function y(x).
Structure: Composition, inverses, domain and range matter before learning formulas.

maths.title: Polynomials
maths.subtitle: Powers with coefficients
summary: Polynomials combine a variable using addition, multiplication and nonnegative integer powers. Their roots and factors carry rich structure.
details: Degree: Linear and quadratic equations have classical solution methods; cubic and quartic formulas came later.
Limits of formulas: There is no general formula using only radicals for every polynomial of degree five or more.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

maths.title: Proof & deduction
maths.subtitle: Why a claim must follow
summary: A proof establishes a conclusion from stated assumptions using valid logical steps. It can be checked without polling every example.
details: Methods: Direct proof, contradiction, contraposition, induction and construction are different tools.
Status language: On this map green means an established definition or theorem, not that every possible question in that branch is finished.

maths.title: Formal logic
maths.subtitle: Precise rules for reasoning
summary: Logic formalises connectives, quantifiers, inference and truth. It distinguishes a statement's form from the topic being discussed.
details: Propositional & predicate: Predicate logic uses "for all" and "there exists" to talk about objects and relations.
Models: Semantics and proof theory are connected, but truth in a model and derivability from axioms are not identical ideas.

sources.title: Open Logic Project: formal logic textbooks
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: classical logic

maths.title: Set theory
maths.subtitle: Collections with membership
summary: Sets collect objects under a membership relation. Modern axiomatic set theory provides a common foundation for much mathematics.
details: Infinity becomes mathematical: Cantor compared infinite sets using one-to-one correspondences rather than finite counting alone.
Do not allow arbitrary collections: The set of all sets that do not contain themselves is not a set in standard axiomatic set theory; unrestricted comprehension leads to paradox.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: set theory
Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Axioms & foundations
maths.subtitle: The starting rules are explicit
summary: A foundation gives mathematical objects and proofs a shared framework. ZFC is common, but not the only foundation.
details: Choice matters: A theorem depends on its assumptions. A result proved using the axiom of choice should not be described as choice-free.
Not a theory of everything: Foundations organise mathematics; they do not decide which physical theory describes nature.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: set theory
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: proof theory

maths.title: Sizes of infinity
maths.subtitle: Countable & uncountable
summary: Infinite sets can have different cardinalities. The natural numbers are countable; the real numbers are uncountable.
details: Diagonal argument: Any proposed list of all real numbers can be used to construct a real number missing from that list.
Counterintuitive but proved: The integers, even integers and rationals are countable, despite proper inclusions between these sets.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: set theory

maths.title: Gödel’s incompleteness
maths.subtitle: Some truths escape a formal system
summary: Sufficiently strong, effectively axiomatised, consistent formal systems have statements they cannot prove or refute.
details: The qualifications matter: This concerns systems that can represent enough arithmetic; it is not "nothing can be proved".
Consistency: Under the stated hypotheses, such a system cannot prove its own consistency by its own methods. Frauds and oversimplifications often omit these conditions.

maths.title: Computability
maths.subtitle: What can an algorithm decide?
summary: Computability studies which functions and questions have effective procedures, independently of how fast a modern computer is.
details: Undecidability: There is no general algorithm that decides whether every possible program halts on every input.
Model of computation: Turing machines are a precise mathematical model, not a claim that every physical device is a Turing machine.

maths.title: Number theory
maths.subtitle: Patterns in integers
summary: Number theory studies integers and their generalisations, including divisibility, primes, congruences and equations with integer solutions.
details: Proofs & patterns: Many statements can be checked for many examples yet remain unproved in general. Green results and red conjectures stay separate here.
Connections: The subject connects algebra, geometry, analysis, computation and cryptography.

sources.title: MacTutor: history of arithmetic and number theory
Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Prime numbers
maths.subtitle: Multiplicative building blocks
summary: A prime greater than 1 has exactly two positive divisors. Every positive integer above 1 factors into primes uniquely, up to order.
details: Infinitely many: Euclid's proof uses a finite list of primes to construct a number requiring a prime outside that list.
Distribution: Infinitude is known; many detailed distribution patterns remain active research.

sources.title: Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Modular arithmetic
maths.subtitle: Arithmetic with remainders
summary: Two integers are congruent modulo n when their difference is divisible by n. This is arithmetic on cyclic remainder classes.
details: Clock idea: The clock analogy helps, but modular arithmetic includes much more than hours.
Applications: Congruences underpin divisibility tests, cryptography and many parts of algebra and number theory.

sources.title: Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction
Khan Academy: modular arithmetic and publicly shared codes

maths.title: Fermat’s Last Theorem
maths.subtitle: A famous problem — solved
summary: For n > 2, there are no positive integers a, b, c with aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ.
details: Breakthrough: Andrew Wiles published his proof in 1995; a gap in the initial approach was repaired with Richard Taylor.
Beyond the statement: The proof used deep links between elliptic curves and modular forms. The short elementary statement does not imply a short elementary proof.
Solved record: This is deliberately green. It is not an open bounty.

sources.title: Wiles: Modular elliptic curves and Fermat’s Last Theorem (1995)
Taylor & Wiles: Ring-theoretic properties of Hecke algebras (1995)

maths.title: Twin prime conjecture
maths.subtitle: Prime pairs two apart forever?
summary: Are there infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by exactly 2? No accepted proof or disproof exists.
details: Real partial progress: Zhang proved bounded prime gaps in 2013; Maynard, Tao and the Polymath8 collaboration reduced a proven bound to 246.
Do not blur the gap: A bounded gap of 246 is not a gap of 2. The twin-prime statement remains open.

sources.title: Maynard: Small gaps between primes (Annals of Mathematics, 2015)
AMS: small and bounded prime gaps (survey)

maths.title: Goldbach’s conjecture
maths.subtitle: Even numbers as prime sums
summary: The strong binary Goldbach conjecture says every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes.
details: Checked is not proved: Computer checks over finite ranges do not settle every even integer.
Different statement: Results for sums of three primes or almost-primes are important but are not a proof of the binary conjecture.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld: selected unsolved problems and current status

maths.title: Collatz conjecture
maths.subtitle: A simple rule, no general proof
summary: Halve an even positive integer; apply 3n + 1 to an odd one. Must every starting number eventually reach 1?
details: Simple to state: The rule is elementary. Extensive computation is not a proof for all positive integers.
Status: No accepted general proof or counterexample is documented by the reference here. This map assigns no probability to its truth.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld: selected unsolved problems and current status
Lagarias: The 3x+1 problem and its generalizations (1985)

maths.title: Riemann hypothesis
maths.subtitle: Zeros of the zeta function
summary: The conjecture says every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2.
details: Why primes are involved: The zeta function relates analysis to the distribution of primes through products and explicit formulas.
Precision: "All zeros" is wrong without "nontrivial"; negative even integers are known trivial zeros. Numerical checks do not settle the conjecture.
Prize status: Clay lists the Riemann Hypothesis as unsolved, checked 6 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Clay Mathematics Institute: Millennium Prize Problems

maths.title: Probability
maths.subtitle: A precise model of chance
summary: Probability assigns numerical likelihoods to events under a specified model. It does not predict a guaranteed individual outcome.
details: Foundations: Modern probability uses a sample space, events and a probability measure satisfying Kolmogorov's axioms.
Interpretations vary: Frequency and degree-of-belief interpretations can motivate different uses of the same calculus.

sources.title: Kolmogorov: Foundations of the Theory of Probability (English translation)

maths.title: Random variables
maths.subtitle: Chance mapped to numbers
summary: A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome. Its distribution describes probabilities of possible values.
details: Not a fluctuating variable: The word random refers to the probability model. A distribution describes long-run or modelled probabilities.
Expectation: A mean is a weighted average, not a promise about a single observation or a finite run.

sources.title: Kolmogorov: Foundations of the Theory of Probability (English translation)

maths.title: Statistics & inference
maths.subtitle: Learn from data without certainty
summary: Statistics summarises data and infers properties of a model or population under assumptions. Uncertainty is quantified, not erased.
details: Uncertainty: A confidence interval has a precise repeated-sampling interpretation. A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Data limitations: Bias, sampling design, measurement, model mismatch and multiple testing can all affect conclusions.

sources.title: American Statistical Association: statement on p-values

maths.title: Conditional probability & Bayes
maths.subtitle: Update with evidence
summary: Conditional probability updates a model when information is known. Bayes' theorem reverses conditional relationships.
details: Formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), when P(B) > 0.
Important distinction: P(A|B) need not equal P(B|A): a test's sensitivity is not the same as the probability of having a condition after a positive test.

sources.title: Kolmogorov: Foundations of the Theory of Probability (English translation)

maths.title: Information & entropy
maths.subtitle: Uncertainty in bits
summary: Shannon entropy measures uncertainty in a probability distribution. For bits, H = −Σ p log₂ p.
details: What it means: Entropy is not a measure of semantic meaning or truth. The distribution and question matter.
Compression & channels: Information theory gives fundamental limits for compression and communication; practical implementations remain engineering design.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

maths.title: Codes & compression
maths.subtitle: Represent information efficiently
summary: Coding represents symbols so they can be stored, transmitted or recovered. Compression can exploit predictable patterns.
details: Two kinds: Lossless codes preserve exact data; lossy schemes discard some information under fidelity criteria.
Limits: No lossless method can shorten every possible input; pigeonhole rules forbid that universal promise.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

maths.title: Error-correcting codes
maths.subtitle: Add structure to survive noise
summary: Redundancy can let a receiver detect or correct transmission errors without receiving a clean original stream first.
details: Trade-offs: Rate, distance, noise and decoding complexity determine what a code can achieve.
Connections: Algebra, combinatorics, probability and geometry all contribute to modern coding theory.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
Hamming: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes (1950)

maths.title: Limits & continuity
maths.subtitle: Approach a value precisely
summary: A limit describes behaviour as inputs approach a point. Continuity rules out specified kinds of jumps at a point.
details: Epsilon–delta: The formal definition quantifies how close outputs must be and how close inputs need to be to achieve it.
Not just substitution: Direct substitution works for continuous functions, but limits also treat cases where the function is undefined at the point.

maths.title: Derivatives
maths.subtitle: Instantaneous change
summary: A derivative is a limit of average changes. It measures a function's local linear change.
details: Notation: dy/dx is notation for a derivative, not literally a fraction in every context; treating it as one without care can mislead.
Geometry & modelling: Slopes, velocities, sensitivities and optimisation all use derivatives.

maths.title: Integrals
maths.subtitle: Accumulate small contributions
summary: Integration combines local contributions into area, mass, probability and other totals. Different definitions handle different functions.
details: Fundamental theorem: Differentiation and integration are linked under clear hypotheses. Approximation, computation and antiderivatives are not always the same task.
Lebesgue theory: Measure and Lebesgue integration extend analysis to broad classes of functions and underpin modern probability.

maths.title: Sequences & series
maths.subtitle: Add infinitely many terms, carefully
summary: An infinite series has a sum when its sequence of partial sums converges. Rearrangement and approximation need care.
details: Power series: Some functions match a power series only on a stated interval; outside it, the same expression may diverge or represent something else.
Taylor series: A Taylor expansion can give local approximations, but existence of every derivative does not automatically guarantee equality to the series.

maths.title: Differential equations
maths.subtitle: Rules for how a system changes
summary: An ordinary differential equation relates a function to its derivatives. It encodes a rule of change, not just a static shape.
details: Initial conditions: Existence and uniqueness depend on assumptions; a differential equation alone may have many solutions.
Qualitative behaviour: Stability, equilibrium and numerical approximation matter even without a formula for the solution.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics: ordinary differential equations

maths.title: Vector calculus
maths.subtitle: Change through space
summary: Gradient, divergence and curl describe how scalar and vector fields vary through space.
details: Integral theorems: Green, Stokes and divergence theorems connect boundary behaviour to accumulated change inside a region, with regularity assumptions.
Physics: Fields, flux and conservation laws use this language; the mathematics alone does not choose a physical law.

maths.title: Partial differential equations
maths.subtitle: Change across space and time
summary: PDEs involve partial derivatives in more than one independent variable. Waves, heat and fluids are standard examples.
details: Different types: Elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic equations have different behaviours, but real problems can mix types.
General open questions: Many individual PDE problems are solved. Others, including global regularity questions for particular equations, remain open.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics: partial differential equations
Clay Mathematics Institute: Millennium Prize Problems

maths.title: Dynamical systems & chaos
maths.subtitle: Simple rules, hard predictions
summary: Dynamical systems study how states evolve. Sensitive dependence can make long-range numerical prediction difficult even in deterministic models.
details: Not randomness by definition: Chaos is not a synonym for randomness. The equations can be deterministic while sensitive to initial conditions.
Measures of behaviour: Attractors, bifurcations and stability help describe whole families of trajectories.

maths.title: Groups
maths.subtitle: One operation + symmetry
summary: A group has an associative operation, an identity and inverses. It captures reversible symmetry, commutative or not.
details: Examples: Integer addition, nonzero real multiplication, rotations and permutations form groups under their specified operations.
Representation: A group can act on another object or vector space instead of appearing only as an abstract multiplication table.

maths.title: Rings & fields
maths.subtitle: Two operations, compatible rules
summary: Rings support addition and multiplication under axioms. Fields also permit division by every nonzero element.
details: Examples: Integers form a ring; rational, real and complex numbers form fields. Matrix rings generally have noncommutative multiplication.
Ideals & quotients: Ideals generalise divisibility and let new structures be built from old ones.

maths.title: Galois theory
maths.subtitle: Symmetries of equations
summary: Galois theory relates field extensions to groups of symmetries. It explains when roots can be expressed using radicals.
details: Degree-five boundary: There is no universal radical formula for all quintic polynomials, although many particular quintics are solvable by radicals.
Broader impact: The ideas reach far beyond the original root-formula question into number theory and geometry.

maths.title: Lie groups & representations
maths.subtitle: Continuous symmetry
summary: Lie groups combine smooth geometry and group structure. Representations describe their actions as linear transformations.
details: Examples: Rotations, unitary groups and Lorentz transformations provide continuous symmetries.
Physics: The Standard Model uses gauge symmetry, including SU(3), SU(2) and U(1); this mathematical structure does not alone derive the measured particle content.

sources.title: David Tong: Lectures on the Standard Model

maths.title: Topology
maths.subtitle: Closeness without a ruler
summary: Topology studies continuity, neighbourhoods and properties preserved by continuous deformation, without requiring a metric.
details: Open sets: A topology specifies which sets are open; the resulting space can support continuity even when distance is undefined.
Important warning: Topological equivalence is not literally "tearing or gluing allowed". Homeomorphisms are continuous bijections with continuous inverse.

maths.title: Manifolds
maths.subtitle: Locally like flat space
summary: A manifold is modelled locally on Euclidean space. It can be curved globally even though small coordinate patches look flat.
details: Charts & atlases: Coordinates describe patches. Smoothness comes from compatible transitions, not from one preferred coordinate grid.
Generalisation: Spheres, tori and many curved spaces are examples; manifolds may have any dimension.

maths.title: Riemannian geometry
maths.subtitle: Measure length on curved spaces
summary: A Riemannian metric gives each tangent space an inner product that varies smoothly, enabling lengths, angles and curvature.
details: Relativity nuance: Spacetime in general relativity is Lorentzian, not Riemannian. It uses pseudo-Riemannian geometry, a generalisation with a different metric signature.
Cross-link: The map therefore labels the physics relationship "differential geometry → general relativity", not "Riemannian geometry is spacetime".

sources.title: Sean Carroll: lecture notes on general relativity

maths.title: Curvature
maths.subtitle: Geometry that need not be flat
summary: Curvature measures how a surface or space departs from flatness, and can be intrinsic rather than depending on an outside space.
details: Parallel transport: Moving a vector consistently around a curved space can change its direction after a loop.
General relativity: Curvature of spacetime enters Einstein's field equations; matter and energy are related to that curvature.

sources.title: Sean Carroll: lecture notes on general relativity

maths.title: Knot theory
maths.subtitle: Loops that cannot be untied
summary: Mathematical knots are closed loops in space, studied up to continuous deformation of the surrounding space.
details: Invariants: Polynomials and other invariants can distinguish some knots, but a single invariant usually does not classify every knot.
Applications: Connections include topology, quantum field theory and molecular biology; not every proposed physical application is established.

maths.title: Poincaré conjecture
maths.subtitle: A three-dimensional sphere test — solved
summary: Every simply connected, closed three-manifold is homeomorphic to the three-sphere.
details: Proof route: Perelman used Hamilton's Ricci-flow programme, with results announced in 2002 and 2003.
Bigger result: The work also proves Thurston's geometrisation conjecture, which has the Poincaré conjecture as a special case.
Status: Clay recognises this as the solved Millennium Prize problem. Checked 6 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Perelman: The entropy formula for the Ricci flow (2002)

maths.title: Combinatorics
maths.subtitle: Counting structured possibilities
summary: Combinatorics counts, arranges and analyses discrete structures without necessarily listing every possibility.
details: Examples: Permutations, combinations, binomial coefficients, inclusion–exclusion and recurrence relations answer different counting questions.
Exact vs asymptotic: An exact count and a large-size estimate are different, both valuable, kinds of result.

sources.title: Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Graph theory
maths.subtitle: Things and their connections
summary: A graph has vertices and edges. It models networks, paths, colourings and connectivity independently of its physical layout.
details: Simple definitions vary: Some definitions allow loops or multiple edges; an exact problem statement must say which graphs are allowed.
Algorithms: Searching, shortest paths, flow and matching combine structural theory with computation.

sources.title: Euler: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (1736; Stony Brook translation of the original paper)
Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Trees & spanning structures
maths.subtitle: Connected without cycles
summary: A finite tree is a connected acyclic graph. Between any two vertices is exactly one path.
details: Equivalent viewpoint: A finite connected graph with n vertices and n−1 edges is a tree.
Map analogy: The maths tree is a curated learning map, not a literal classification of every theorem or field of mathematics.

sources.title: Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction

maths.title: Four-colour theorem
maths.subtitle: Map regions need only four
summary: Every planar map can be coloured with four colours so neighbouring regions do not share a colour.
details: Precise assumptions: Regions must be contiguous, with finite border requirements as formalised in graph theory. Countries with disconnected pieces are a different problem.
Computer-assisted proof: The proof was an influential landmark for computer checking in mathematics, not a mere exhaustive drawing of every map.

sources.title: Appel & Haken: Every planar map is four colorable, Part I (1977)

maths.title: Ramsey theory
maths.subtitle: Order inside enough disorder
summary: Ramsey theory asks when sufficiently large structures must contain specified ordered substructures.
details: Famous example: At a party of six people, some three people are mutual acquaintances or mutual strangers, for the standard complete-graph two-colouring version.
Still active: Many exact Ramsey numbers remain unknown despite the existence theorems being proved.

sources.title: Ramsey: On a Problem of Formal Logic (1930; Oxford Academic)

maths.title: Optimisation
maths.subtitle: Best choice under constraints
summary: Optimisation seeks an allowed input that minimises or maximises a specified objective.
details: Local ≠ global: A stationary point is not necessarily a global optimum; convexity can supply stronger guarantees.
Discrete & continuous: Linear programming, convex optimisation and combinatorial optimisation have different tools and limits.

sources.title: Boyd & Vandenberghe: Convex Optimization (free author copy)

maths.title: Fourier analysis
maths.subtitle: Waves built from simpler waves
summary: Fourier methods represent functions using oscillations or frequency components. They connect signals, heat, probability and differential equations.
details: Convergence is nuanced: Pointwise, uniform and mean-square convergence are different; an infinite trigonometric series does not automatically equal its originating function everywhere.
Transforms: Fourier transforms can turn differentiation into multiplication, revealing frequency structure and simplifying some equations.

maths.title: Complex analysis
maths.subtitle: Differentiation in the complex plane
summary: Complex differentiability has much stronger consequences than real differentiability. Analytic functions are deeply linked to contour integration.
details: Cauchy theory: Under stated conditions, contour integrals relate to enclosed singularities through residues.
Connections: Analytic continuation, entire functions and poles are essential tools in number theory and mathematical physics.

maths.title: Zeta & L-functions
maths.subtitle: Analysis encodes arithmetic
summary: Dirichlet series associate analytic functions with arithmetic sequences. The Riemann zeta function is a central example.
details: Euler product: For Re(s)>1, ζ(s)=Σ1/nˢ equals a product over primes. This is one precise link between primes and analysis.
Analytic continuation: The zeta function extends beyond the original series domain, but the series itself does not converge everywhere.

maths.title: Elliptic curves
maths.subtitle: Cubic equations with group structure
summary: Elliptic curves are smooth cubic curves with a specified base point and a geometric group law. Over different fields they have different behaviours.
details: Arithmetic: Their rational points connect number theory, algebra and complex analysis. They are not the same thing as ellipses.
Cryptography: Finite-field elliptic curves support cryptographic protocols; their security depends on implementation and computational assumptions.

maths.title: Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer
maths.subtitle: Rational points from an L-function?
summary: The conjecture relates the rank of an elliptic curve's rational points to the order of vanishing of its L-function at s=1.
details: A bridge: It links a discrete arithmetic invariant to an analytic object. Important special cases are proved; the full conjecture is not.
Status: Clay lists the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture as unsolved, checked 6 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Clay Mathematics Institute: Millennium Prize Problems

maths.title: Algebraic geometry
maths.subtitle: Geometry of polynomial solutions
summary: Algebraic geometry studies solution sets of polynomial equations using algebra, geometry and modern structural languages.
details: Fields matter: Solutions over the complex numbers, real numbers, rational numbers and finite fields can behave quite differently.
Modern language: Varieties, ideals, schemes and sheaves are successive tools; the map only introduces the landscape.

sources.title: The Stacks Project: open algebraic-geometry reference

maths.title: Hodge conjecture
maths.subtitle: Topology from algebraic cycles?
maths.date: W. V. D. Hodge · mid-20th c.
summary: For a smooth complex projective variety, the conjecture characterises certain rational cohomology classes as rational combinations of classes of algebraic cycles.
details: Not all topology: It does not claim every feature of every space comes from algebraic equations. Smooth projective complex varieties and Hodge classes matter.
Known cases ≠ general proof: Some special cases are established. Clay lists the general conjecture as unsolved, checked 6 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Clay Mathematics Institute: Millennium Prize Problems

maths.title: Category theory
maths.subtitle: Objects + arrows + composition
summary: Category theory studies objects through their relationships, with arrows that compose associatively and identities at each object.
details: Structure-preserving maps: Examples include sets with functions, groups with homomorphisms, and topological spaces with continuous maps.
Not just abstraction: Functors, natural transformations and universal properties reveal shared patterns across fields without claiming all objects are the same.

sources.title: Mac Lane: Categories for the Working Mathematician (Springer)

maths.title: Topos & categorical logic
maths.subtitle: A setting for variable sets
summary: A topos shares useful properties with the category of sets and can interpret a form of higher-order logic.
details: Different logic: A general topos need not obey classical logic or the axiom of choice. One should not assume every set-theoretic rule transfers unchanged.
Applications: The language appears in algebraic geometry, topology and foundations. This card is a pointer, not a complete definition.

sources.title: Mac Lane & Moerdijk: Sheaves in Geometry and Logic (Springer)

maths.title: Homotopy & higher structure
maths.subtitle: Deform paths and maps
summary: Homotopy compares maps by continuous deformation. Homotopy groups record holes and higher-dimensional structure.
details: Fundamental group: Loops based at a point, up to homotopy, form a group under composition.
Frontier: Higher-category and homotopy-invariant methods are active tools across topology, algebra and mathematical physics; this map introduces them only as established frameworks.

maths.title: Algorithms
maths.subtitle: Finite procedures for a task
summary: An algorithm is an effective procedure with explicit input, steps and output. Correctness and resource use require separate analysis.
details: Not just code: Euclidean division is an algorithm; a Turing machine is one formal model for expressing algorithms.
Analysis: Worst-case, average-case and amortised bounds can differ. A fast empirical test does not replace a complexity statement.

sources.title: Levin: Discrete Mathematics — an Open Introduction
Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein: Introduction to Algorithms

maths.title: Computational complexity
maths.subtitle: Resources needed to solve
summary: Complexity theory classifies problems by resources such as time, memory or communication, as input size grows.
details: Problems, not programs: The target is intrinsic resource requirements under a model, not whether one implementation seems fast.
Asymptotic notation: Big-O describes an upper growth bound, not an exact runtime or a guarantee for small inputs.

sources.title: Cook: The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures (1971)

maths.title: P versus NP
maths.subtitle: Easy to check means easy to solve?
summary: P is efficiently solvable decision problems; NP is decision problems with efficiently verifiable certificates. Does P = NP?
details: Not a speed benchmark: "Efficient" has a precise polynomial-time meaning here. NP does not stand for "not polynomial".
Consequences: If one NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm then all NP problems do. No accepted general resolution is known.
Status: Clay lists P vs NP as unsolved, checked 6 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Cook: The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures (1971)

maths.title: Cryptography
maths.subtitle: Security from hard structure
summary: Modern cryptography designs protocols with explicit security goals, adversary models and computational assumptions.
details: Public key: Some systems depend on the presumed difficulty of computational problems. That is not the same as proving those problems hard.
Quantum impact: Shor's algorithm would break widely used factoring and discrete-log schemes on a sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer; that machine is not assumed to exist here.

sources.title: Katz & Lindell: Introduction to Modern Cryptography
Shor: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms

maths.title: Quantum information
maths.subtitle: Bits become quantum states
summary: Quantum information studies storage, transmission and processing using quantum states, measurement and entanglement.
details: Different resource: Qubits are described in Hilbert spaces. Measurement outcomes are probabilistic under the rules of quantum mechanics.
Quantum entropy: Von Neumann entropy is the quantum analogue for density operators. It has different operational meanings from ordinary Shannon entropy.

sources.title: Nielsen & Chuang: Quantum Computation and Quantum Information

maths.title: Numerical analysis
maths.subtitle: Approximate answers reliably
summary: Numerical analysis designs algorithms for approximation and studies accuracy, stability, convergence and computational cost.
details: Rounding: Floating-point arithmetic is not exact real arithmetic. More digits can help but do not automatically cure an unstable method.
Verification: Error bounds, conditioning and independent tests matter more than an impressive number of displayed decimal places.

maths.title: Yang–Mills & the mass gap
maths.subtitle: Make quantum gauge theory rigorous
summary: The problem asks for a mathematically rigorous quantum Yang–Mills theory on four-dimensional space with a positive mass gap and established axioms.
details: Physics vs mathematics: Quantum gauge theories are enormously successful physics. That does not amount to the rigorous construction required by this mathematical problem.
Status: Clay lists Yang–Mills & the Mass Gap as unsolved, checked 6 Nov 2026.

maths.title: Navier–Stokes: 3D smoothness
maths.subtitle: Claimed breakthrough; checking continues

maths.title: Kepler conjecture
maths.subtitle: The densest sphere packing — solved
summary: No packing of equal spheres in ordinary three-dimensional space has greater density than the face-centred cubic arrangement.
details: Density: The maximum density is π/√18, about 74%. The proof combines geometry with extensive computation.
Formal checking: The Flyspeck project later produced a formal proof of the result. Publication and formal proof are related but distinct milestones.

Cantor’s first set-theory paper establishes a landmark in the theory of infinite sets.
Cantor’s diagonal argument is presented and appears in a volume dated 1890–91, later printed. The range preserves that bibliographic nuance.

events.text: Wallis presents a geometric representation of complex numbers. A landmark, not the final modern theory.

events.text: Gauss’s Disquisitiones gives a systematic treatment of congruences and arithmetic residues.
Alphonse de Polignac publishes a more general prime-gap conjecture that includes infinitely many prime pairs differing by two.
Christian Goldbach and Leonhard Euler’s correspondence gives the statement now associated with Goldbach’s name.

events.text: The Collatz problem circulated in the twentieth century and is often dated to 1937; the first journal appearance is later. The date is not presented as exact.

events.text: Ancient mathematical traditions used right-triangle relationships. This is not a claimed discovery year assigned to Pythagoras.

events.label: c. 5th century BCE → medieval astronomy
events.text: Trigonometry developed through Greek, Indian, Islamic and other astronomical traditions. No single inventor/date is assigned.
Lobachevsky publishes non-Euclidean geometry in 1829; Bolyai follows in 1832.

events.text: Elliptic-curve arithmetic has many historical layers; this range marks their modern development without crediting all of them to one person.

events.text: Gauss’s investigations of curved surfaces are a landmark. Riemann’s 1854 geometry lecture is a separate anchor.

events.text: Francis Guthrie poses the four-colour question.
Appel and Haken publish the computer-assisted proof. The original paper appeared in 1977; later formal verification is a separate milestone.

events.text: Henri Poincaré poses the conjecture in his fifth complement to Analysis Situs.
Grigori Perelman announces the proof in preprints posted in 2002 and 2003.
Poincaré’s Analysis Situs is a foundational landmark in algebraic topology.
Poincaré’s fundamental-group and topology work is a landmark; higher homotopy theory developed later.
Tait’s On Knots is the map’s dated knot-table landmark, not a claim that knots had never been studied before.
Riemann’s geometry lecture is the historical anchor for the card.
Eilenberg and Mac Lane publish General Theory of Natural Equivalences.

events.label: 1832 · manuscript; 1846 published
events.text: Galois leaves his group-theoretic ideas in a manuscript in 1832; Liouville publishes Galois’s work in 1846.
Lie-group and representation theory are treated as parts of a broader development, not as simultaneous discoveries.

events.label: 1950 · proceedings published 1952
events.text: W. V. D. Hodge presents the conjecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians; its proceedings appear later.
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer develop and publish the conjecture as a range of work, not a single-day announcement.
Fermat and Pascal’s correspondence on the problem of points is a landmark in probability theory.
Thomas Bayes’s essay is published posthumously by Richard Price.

events.text: Cauchy’s approach to rigorous limits is a historical progression, culminating here in the 1821 Cours d’analyse.
Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse is a landmark in rigorous convergence and series theory.

events.label: early 19th century · 1807/1822
events.text: Fourier’s work on heat developed through a memoir and later 1822 publication. The range makes the chronology explicit.
Riemann’s geometry lecture supplies the map’s historical anchor for manifold ideas.
Dedekind publishes a rigorous construction of real numbers using cuts.

sources.title: MacTutor: the real numbers and their history

events.text: Numerical analysis is a broad development, not a single dated invention.
Navier and Stokes contribute to the equations; these are publication dates.
Clay formulates the existence-and-smoothness prize problem. Later claimed work must not be treated as accepted resolution.
Yang and Mills publish their equations.
Clay formulates the rigorous quantum Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap prize problem.
Euler’s zeta product, Dirichlet’s 1837 L-functions, and Riemann’s 1859 paper are separate landmarks for this broad node.

Cook’s theorem gives a precise anchor for the P versus NP problem; independent Soviet work also matters.

events.text: This paper’s selected combinatorics anchor is the Pascal–Fermat problem-of-points correspondence. Discrete enumeration itself has older traditions.

events.text: Ancient arithmetic records include fractions and ratios. The modern number concept evolved across cultures.

Frege publishes Begriffsschrift. Aristotle is not replaced as a historical root by this publication milestone.

events.text: Leibniz’s printed differential-calculus work is the selected anchor; Newton’s work and notation are separate parts of the history.

events.label: 1686 · later integral theories follow
events.text: This is the early-calculus publication anchor, not a claim that all integrals date from Leibniz’s paper. Riemann and Lebesgue milestones are later.
D’Alembert’s vibrating-string work is a dated differential-equation example. Ordinary differential equations arose through wider calculus work.

events.text: Green’s mathematical-analysis essay is a dated landmark in the history of integral field theorems.
D’Alembert publishes his vibrating-string analysis containing the wave equation; the full subject develops much later.
Lorenz publishes Deterministic nonperiodic flow. Poincaré and other earlier dynamical work remains acknowledged.
